name: Wilson's theorem
whenToUse: A factorial appears modulo a prime, especially one just below the prime.
pitfall: It is about $(p - 1)!$, not $p!$ (which is $0$ modulo $p$). For composite $n > 4$, $(n - 1)! \equiv 0 \pmod n$.
derivation: Each number from $2$ to $p - 2$ pairs with a different inverse in that range, so those pairs multiply to $1$. What is left is $1 \cdot (p - 1) \equiv -1$.
